hero.eyebrow: AN OPEN VIEW OF WORK IN INDIA
hero.title: India at Work.
hero.description: Labour-market data, translated into something people can actually understand — and use.

why.label: Why data matters
why.text: Numbers are not just numbers. They shape how we understand jobs, inequality, participation and opportunity — and help us ask better questions about what is changing.

glance.title: A few numbers can change the frame.
glance.description: Start with the indicators that anchor the story: GDP growth, youth unemployment and labour-force participation.
glance.eprText: The share of the working-age population participating in the labour force.
glance.yuText: Young people in the labour force who are currently without work.
glance.lfprText: Participation includes people who are working or actively looking for work.
glance.gapText: Male LFPR minus female LFPR, measured in percentage points.

trade.title: Growth and youth employment tell different parts of the story.
trade.description: Comparing endpoints can reveal direction without pretending we know what happened between them.
trade.endpoint: Endpoint comparison only — no intermediate values are fabricated.

youth.title: Participation is not the same as opportunity.
youth.description: A young population can be an economic asset — but only if people can participate, find work and build productive careers.
youth.dividendTitle: A large working-age population creates potential — not an automatic payoff.
youth.dividendText: The demographic dividend depends on people being able to participate productively in the economy. Education, skills, jobs, mobility and institutions all influence whether that potential is realised.
youth.lfpr: Labour Force Participation Rate · two endpoints
youth.femaleCaption: Female LFPR increased from 26.67% in 2013 to 32.43% in 2025.
youth.interpretation: Youth unemployment decreased from 24.47% in 2013 to 16.02% in 2025. This visual uses only supplied endpoint values.

gender.title: The gender gap is visible in one glance.
gender.description: The 2025 labour-force participation rates supplied for this project show a substantial difference between men and women.
gender.caption: Female LFPR increased from 26.67% in 2013 to 32.43% in 2025; the LFPR gap was 49.23 percentage points in 2025.
gender.scale: Common scale: 0–100%. LFPR gender gap = male LFPR minus female LFPR.
gender.question: Where is the gap?

opportunities.title: Turn information into a next step.
opportunities.description: A future-ready opportunity layer can connect people to internships, jobs, fellowships and skills programmes — filtered by what actually matters to them.
opportunities.whereTitle: The goal is not just to show data. It is to make the data useful.
opportunities.whereText: India at Work is designed as an awareness layer: understand the labour market first, then discover relevant pathways into work, training and enterprise.
opportunities.sample: Sample data — live opportunities coming soon

footer.description: An editorial data platform for understanding work, participation and opportunity in India.
footer.note: Data note: labour-market statistics shown here come from the new supplied dataset. Opportunity listings are sample data and are not live vacancies.
footer.methodologyText: The labour-market data source for this update is the new supplied dataset. The supplied dataset covers 1990–2025. Blank cells are retained as unavailable values; no missing values are guessed or interpolated.

accessibility.genderChart: Two horizontal bars on a common zero to one hundred percent scale. Men: 81.65 percent LFPR. Women: 32.43 percent LFPR.
